Business insurance

Business Insurance in Kenya

Business insurance is not one policy. It is a set of covers, each answering a different way your business can lose money: a fire, an injured employee, a customer claim, a stolen delivery, a cyber incident. The right combination depends on what you own, who you employ, what you do and what contracts you have signed.

Request a quoteSpeak to an advisor

General information only. What is covered, the terms and the premium depend on the insurer’s policy wording, your circumstances and the information you disclose. Nothing here is a promise of cover.

What it covers

  • Property and assets: buildings, stock, machinery and contents against fire and other named perils
  • People: work injury cover for employees, and group life or medical benefits where you offer them
  • Liability: claims from third parties, clients or customers for injury, damage or professional error
  • Operations: goods moving by road or sea, business interruption after an insured loss, project risks on site
  • Specialist exposures: cyber incidents, directors and officers liability, fidelity and money risks

Who needs it

  • Owners of shops, restaurants, hotels, clinics, schools, offices and warehouses
  • Contractors, developers and engineering firms
  • Importers, exporters, logistics and transport businesses
  • Consultancies and professional firms
  • Any employer, since work injury cover is a legal duty for most employers

Common risks

Underinsurance

Stock, equipment and buildings are often insured at old values. If a loss happens, a claim can be reduced when the sum insured is lower than the real value.

Gaps between policies

Property cover does not pay a customer injured on your premises, and a liability policy does not repair your building. Gaps usually appear where nobody has looked at the whole programme.

Contract requirements

Tenders, landlords, lenders and large clients often require specific covers and limits. Missing them can cost you the contract.

Important considerations and exclusions

  • Every policy has exclusions, conditions, excesses and limits. Read the schedule and wording, not just the summary.
  • Cover is generally subject to accurate disclosure. Material facts that are not disclosed can affect a claim.
  • Some covers are claims-made or have reporting conditions. Dates matter.
  • Premium figures depend on your risk and the insurer. Any quote is subject to the insurer’s terms.

What affects the premium

  • Type of business and activities
  • Sums insured and asset values
  • Location and construction of premises
  • Number of employees and payroll
  • Claims history
  • Security and fire protection
  • Limits and excesses chosen

Premiums are set by insurers, so we do not publish figures. Tell us about your situation and we will explain what is driving the quotation.

What we need for a quotation

  • Business name, registration type and industry
  • Locations and what each location is used for
  • Asset and stock values
  • Employee numbers and approximate payroll
  • Existing policies and renewal dates, if any
  • Claims in recent years, if any

How Chestnut can help

We explain the cover in plain language, collect the information insurers need, approach suitable insurers for terms, and help with renewals and claims. Policies are issued by insurers, and you decide what to buy.

Frequently asked questions

What insurance does a business in Kenya actually need?

It depends on the business, but most employers need work injury cover (WIBA), and most businesses with premises or stock need property cover. Customer-facing businesses usually need public liability. Professional firms should consider professional indemnity. A short risk review is the quickest way to find your list.

Can I put everything on one policy?

Some insurers offer combined packages for small and medium businesses, which can be convenient. Larger or more specialised risks often need separate covers. The choice depends on what is available from insurers for your type of business.

I already have insurance. Is a review still useful?

Yes. A review compares what you have with what you own and what your contracts require. It looks for gaps, overlaps and values that have gone out of date, ahead of renewal.
